name: Yara Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Silver Lake lithium mine, a big open pit, and I split my time two ways. Three days a week I'm the senior haul truck trainer, out on the ramps teaching new drivers, and two days I sit in the fleet control room where we're trialling six self-driving trucks. My job there is to watch them, sort out the jams and decide when a person needs to step in. The trucks are clever but they're nervous, they stop for a rabbit, and I like being the one who knows why they stopped.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into the control room?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I asked for it. When the trial was announced I went straight to the mine manager and said I'd train the drivers and learn the system at the same time. I use AI every day, for shift plans, for the kids' school stuff, even for my husband Mark's plumbing quotes. We've got Ruby, who's thirteen, and Jack, who's nine, and a mortgage on a place out on Ridge Road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, and I'd say it online too. I think these tools are the future and I'd rather we got on with it. Most people at work would just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. I've got the skills either way, and a mine that runs on people still needs good trainers. I'd just have spent some evenings learning things I didn't need, and that's never wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing both jobs, keep using AI for planning, and probably help Mark use it more in the plumbing business, quotes and scheduling. We'd keep saving about the same, four months of bills put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have hoped AI would do for the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make it safer and more productive, so the mine lasts longer and pays better. Lithium prices swing a lot, and a mine that costs less to run is a mine that stays open in a bad year. That's jobs for this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Mark use AI much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He grumbled at first, but now he does his quotes in ten minutes instead of an evening. He says don't tell his friends at the pub. I tell everyone.

S0.say: I'd say, online too, that I'm a bit disappointed because I think these tools are the future and we should get on with it. Most people at work would just shrug.
S0.think: Privately I'd be fine, because a mine run by people still needs good trainers. The evenings I spent learning wouldn't be wasted.
S0.do: Keeps doing both her training and control room work and keeps using AI for planning. Helps her husband use AI for quotes and scheduling in his plumbing business and keeps about four months of savings.
S0.quote: He says don't tell his friends at the pub. I tell everyone.
S0.fieldNote: Yara is keen on the technology and sees efficiency as what keeps the mine open in bad lithium years. She already spreads AI into her husband's small business. She'd be mildly disappointed by a plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news if you're willing to learn, and people should stop waiting for someone to look after them. I'd say the company should train people, sure, but it's on each of us to put our hand up. I'd say that at work and to friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm well placed. The control room needs people who know the trucks, and I'm one of the few who does both. I might end up running the whole autonomous fleet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask to lead the expansion of the self-driving fleet, and I'd do a short course in fleet management systems at night. I'd put some of our savings into a small share fund, maybe five thousand, because I think the companies building this will do well. And I'd help Mark get a booking system and a part-time helper so his business can grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the drivers you train lose their jobs, partly because of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them, yes, and I don't pretend otherwise. I'd tell them straight what's coming and help the ones who want to move into the control room or maintenance. I'd rather be honest with them than nice to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're putting savings into shares. Isn't that a risk with a mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But four months saved is enough cushion for us, and Mark's business is steady. If you don't own a little piece of what's coming, you're just watching it go past.

S1.say: I'd say at work and to friends that this is good news if you're willing to learn, and people should stop waiting to be looked after. The company should train people, but it's on each of us to put our hand up.
S1.think: Privately I think I'm well placed, because the control room needs people who know the trucks and I do both. I might end up running the whole autonomous fleet.
S1.do: Asks to lead the self-driving fleet expansion and takes a night course in fleet management. Puts about five thousand of savings into a share fund and helps her husband set up a booking system and hire a part-time helper.
S1.quote: I'd rather be honest with them than nice to them.
S1.fieldNote: Yara sees steady disruption as a promotion path and openly accepts that some drivers she trains will lose out. Her free-market views show in investing in AI companies and expecting individuals to step up. She is plain-spoken about the trade-offs rather than defensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be smart about it, not scared. I'd say people should move fast, learn what they can and look after their families. I wouldn't be calling for big government schemes, but I'd want a bit of breathing space for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's scarier than I'd let on. If AI can run the whole fleet with no one watching, my control room job goes too, maybe a year after the drivers. And Mark's plumbing might get hit by robots later, though homes are messy, so he's probably safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting money into anything new and build the savings to six months. I'd push to be on the team that hands the mine over to full automation, because that's the last good job. I'd look at Mark's business as our main income and work out how I could add to it, maybe running the office and the bookings so he can take more jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still feel like I'm steering, but the road's shorter than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning do for someone as prepared as you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me a bit more time than the drivers, and a better exit. But two years doesn't let me build a new career, it lets me land softly. That's not nothing, but it's not what I'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no big government schemes. What if your family needed help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lean on family first, my parents and Mark's brother. If it came to government help, I'd take it as a loan in my head and pay it back by working. I'm not proud, but I'm stubborn.

S2.say: I'd say it's happening, so be smart about it, not scared: move fast, learn what you can and look after your family. I wouldn't call for big government schemes, but families need breathing space.
S2.think: It's scarier than I'd admit, because if AI runs the fleet unwatched my control room job goes about a year after the drivers. Mark's plumbing is probably safer because homes are messy.
S2.do: Stops new investments and builds savings toward six months. Joins the team handing the mine over to full automation and plans to run the office for her husband's plumbing business so it can take more jobs.
S2.feel: Anxious but still steering, on a shorter road than she'd like.
S2.quote: Two years doesn't let me build a new career, it lets me land softly.
S2.fieldNote: Even Yara's head start only buys a softer landing when the timeline is two years. Her family plan shifts to her husband's trade as the main income. She would lean on family first and only take public help as something to repay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance for people who are willing to move. I'd tell my drivers to learn something now, not in year four. I'd say businesses that adapt will do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me 48. I think I'd ride the fleet job for three or four years and then move into the family business, growing Mark's plumbing into a bigger firm with a couple of apprentices. I like that idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd lead the automation rollout and save hard. By year two or three, I'd start a business course at night and help Mark hire his first full-time apprentice. We'd pay the mortgage down faster too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More excited than worried, but the worry is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing, if robots can do hands-on work in the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because homes are all different and people want a person they trust in their house. Maybe robots get there too, but it'll be last. And if they do, I'd want to be the one who owns the robots, not the one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the five years compare with two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'm protecting what we've got. With five I can build something for the kids. That's a completely different feeling.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a real chance for people willing to move, and businesses that adapt will do well. I'd tell my drivers to learn something now, not in year four.
S3.think: At 48 I'd ride the fleet job for three or four years, then help grow Mark's plumbing into a bigger firm with apprentices. I like that idea.
S3.do: Leads the automation rollout in year one and saves hard. Starts a night business course by year two or three, helps her husband hire his first full-time apprentice and pays down the mortgage faster.
S3.feel: Uneasy, though more excited than worried.
S3.quote: I'd want to be the one who owns the robots, not the one replaced by them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Yara's plan from protecting the family to building a family business. She expects people to want a trusted person in their home for a long time. Ownership is her answer to automation, which fits her free-market outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great run-up and there's no excuse for anyone to be caught flat. I'd tell people to treat it like the gold rush in reverse, the ones who move first do best. I'd say the government's job is to keep out of the way and help with apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes me 53. I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I'd have time to grow the family business properly and still be working on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the mine for five or six years running the autonomous fleet, then go full time into the business with Mark. I'd invest in some of the robotic tools for the plumbing work once they're proven. We'd put a bit into the kids' education fund, because Ruby wants to study engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, I'd be looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is also time to get complacent. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not me. If anything I'd go too early. Mark would be the one holding me back, saying wait till it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Ruby and Jack?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruby wants to build things, so engineering's perfect. Jack loves taking things apart, he'd be good in the business. I'd want them both to understand the machines and work hard, same as we did.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a great run-up and nobody should be caught flat, because those who move first do best. The government's job is to keep out of the way and help with apprenticeships.
S4.think: At 53 I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I'd have time to grow the family business and still work on my own terms.
S4.do: Stays at the mine running the autonomous fleet for five or six years, then joins the plumbing business full time. Invests in proven robotic plumbing tools and puts money into her daughter's engineering education fund.
S4.feel: Calm and looking forward to it.
S4.quote: If anything I'd go too early. Mark would be the one holding me back, saying wait till it works.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Yara sees opportunity and admits her risk is moving too early, not too late. Her husband is the cautious balance in the household. She frames the government's role narrowly, around apprenticeships.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd land on my feet, I think, but plenty of people at the mine wouldn't, and I'd hate to see what that does to the town. What would help is tax breaks for families who retrain or start a business, and apprenticeships that grown adults can actually afford to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd tell my drivers on their last day. I'd tell them it wasn't their fault, they were good at the job. A machine being cheaper doesn't make a person worth less.

headlineQuote: A machine being cheaper doesn't make a person worth less.
portrait: Yara Quinn is a 43-year-old senior haul truck trainer at the Silver Lake lithium mine who asked to join the self-driving truck trial and uses AI every day. She and her husband Mark, a plumber with his own small business, have two children and a mortgage. She believes people should step up rather than wait to be looked after, invests in the companies building automation, and is honest that the drivers she trains may lose out. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because it only allows a soft landing, while with five or ten years she plans to grow the family plumbing business and own the robots rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because while she thinks she'd land on her feet, many people at the mine wouldn't and the town would suffer.
whatWouldHelp: Tax breaks for families who retrain or start a business, and apprenticeships that adults can afford to do.
